Forest plants, often by streams, or in swamps, where some, like Pandanus helicopus, may form dense thickets; or on sandy or rocky beaches or sometimes on limestone
Nothing is known about the pollination of Malaysian species but those that are heavily scented are likely to be pollinated by bees or beetles

Singapore Suppl. 1 (1978) 208--211) observed the fragrant female heads of P. dubius ‘full of beetles’; and Freycinetia angustifolius is likely to be pollinated by bats as its fragrant inflorescences open at night

Benstonea unguiculata has slightly narrower leaves and longer drupes; as well as longer stamens - but note that Ridley was in error in describing P. parvus as having leaves 3 inches wide

The differences between Pandanus yvanii and P. motleyanus Solms (some colour variation – said to differ in purplish leaf prickles and glaucous undersurfaces) are minimal
Stone (1972) says that in Johor these two taxa occur together and probably intergrade (e.g. Stone 7139) but that specimens from Selangor (P. yvanii) and Borneo (P. motleyanus) appear quite distinct
Pandanus yvanii is a taxon from dense shade along forest streams; P. motleyanus occurs more in the open in swampy sites
We believe these differences in colour to be ecological and not specific, and we believe P. motleyanus is synonymous with P. yvanii

The two were described in the same publication so priority is not involved – note that Solms (1878) himself thought P. militaris was the same as P. motleyanus, and that both, as regards to bracts and flowers, were similar to P. yvanii! (Pandanus fruticosus H.St.John from N Borneo is probably the same as well)
Ridley (1925) felt that Pandanus yvanii was a synonym of P. ridleyi, but due to priority, it is the other way around, as P. yvanii was published in 1878, and P. ridleyi in 1904
The lectotype of P. ridleyi (Ridley 10439) had been collected from Bukit Mandi, Singapore, on 22 May 1900
Another collection at SING [SING0180352] bears the same collection number and represents a remaining syntype of Freycinetia valida
Ridley collected it at the same locality but in Aug. 1899
Pandanus militaris and P. yvanii are close
Stone (1972), describing his P. militaris var. malayanus, stated this was close to P. yvanii
He cited as differences broader and more acuminate leaves
Again, P. militaris specimens seem to be from more open situations, so we believe that these taxa are synonymous
The name P. yvanii has priority
We have seen the types of all these taxa, and all of them are rather poor and not very comparable (e.g. fruit only for P. militaris, bracts and a fruit fragment for P. yvanii)
Our preference leaves P. yvanii as a single, widespread and slightly variable species with P. militaris, P. motleyanus and P. ridleyi as synonyms
We believe this situation is better than having several taxa with extremely vague differences and overlapping characters.
